paragraphs: The paper addresses how to decide whether two collections of observations come from different probability distributions. Kernel methods represent each distribution in a mathematical feature space and compare the resulting representations. When that space is sufficiently rich, a zero distance means the distributions are identical. Turning this distance into a statistical test, however, requires knowing how much apparent difference can arise when the distributions actually match.

The main contribution is a consistent estimate of this null distribution, which determines the test's significance threshold. The method uses the eigenvalues of a Gram matrix built from the combined samples. This tackles the difficult distribution of the test statistic through information calculated directly from the observed data.

The estimate can be computed faster than an earlier consistent bootstrap approach. It also has a consistency guarantee that a previous moment-fitting heuristic lacks. Tests on artificial and high-dimensional multivariate data assess its performance. The advance is therefore in calibrating the kernel test reliably and potentially more quickly.
neurips-2009-a-fast-consistent-kernel-tw.tldr: The paper estimates a kernel two-sample test's null distribution consistently from matrix eigenvalues, potentially faster than bootstrap calibration.

paragraphs: The paper studies linear least squares when each unknown must take a value from a finite set. This restriction changes the task from fitting freely adjustable values to choosing among discrete possibilities. The corresponding factor graph is fully connected, creating many loops. The authors report that applying belief propagation directly to this graph gives poor results.

Their approach begins with the Gaussian density associated with the unconstrained linear system. They construct an optimal tree approximation of that density and use it to modify the factor graph. Belief propagation then operates on the modified structure. The distinctive choice is to approximate the continuous Gaussian description rather than directly approximate the exact discrete distribution.

The paper reports that this indirect approximation improves both performance and computational complexity relative to current methods. It demonstrates improved performance on MIMO detection. The result shows that a tractable approximation derived from the unconstrained problem can provide a useful foundation for solving its finite-valued counterpart.
neurips-2009-a-gaussian-tree-approximati.tldr: A tree approximation of an unconstrained Gaussian model makes belief propagation more effective for finite-valued least-squares problems.

paragraphs: The paper examines how strongly unlabeled examples should influence a transductive support vector machine. Its perspective treats ordinary SVM learning and TSVM learning as endpoints: no regularization contributed by unlabeled data versus the full contribution used by TSVM. This distinction concerns the influence of unlabeled data specifically; it does not describe ordinary SVMs as having no regularization at all.

The authors reformulate TSVM so that this influence becomes adjustable. Their formulation includes both original endpoints and allows intermediate settings. This makes partial use of unlabeled information an explicit modeling choice, instead of requiring the learner to accept either endpoint.

They then propose adapting the regularization strength to the data using a smoothness assumption. The underlying idea is that the appropriate influence of unlabeled examples should depend on the structure of the learning problem. Benchmark experiments produce promising results compared with leading TSVM algorithms. These findings support the usefulness of adaptive influence without establishing that one setting or method dominates for every dataset.
neurips-2009-adaptive-regularization-for.tldr: The paper makes the influence of unlabeled data in TSVM adjustable and adapts that influence using a smoothness assumption.

paragraphs: AROW is an online learning algorithm that updates its prediction function as individual training examples arrive. It combines large-margin learning, confidence weighting, and the ability to learn from data that cannot be perfectly separated. This combination addresses a practical difficulty: a learner must continue improving even when the training labels do not permit an error-free separating rule.

The method adapts regularization after each new instance. Its treatment of updates is designed to work especially well when labels contain noise. The paper also connects AROW to existing confidence-weighted online learning techniques, placing its adaptive treatment of the prediction function within that broader approach.

The authors derive a bound on prediction mistakes that does not assume separable data. Its form resembles a bound for the second-order perceptron. Experiments report leading performance and notable robustness on non-separable data. Together, these contributions provide theoretical and empirical support for an online learner that accommodates imperfect labels, without requiring the training problem to be perfectly solvable.
neurips-2009-adaptive-regularization-of-.tldr: AROW adapts regularization during online learning and combines a mistake bound without separability assumptions with empirical robustness to noisy labels.

paragraphs: Recognizing an object in a scene depends on both its own appearance and its relationship to surrounding objects. The paper argues that representing those relationships only through object categories may leave useful contextual information unused. Two individual objects can carry appearance and spatial information that a category-level relationship does not explicitly retain.

The Visual Memex represents objects through exemplars and records relationships between individual instances. Its representation combines local visual appearance with two-dimensional spatial context. This gives scene reasoning access to what particular objects look like and how they are positioned relative to one another, extending the contextual description beyond category identities.

The authors evaluate the model on Torralba's Context Challenge against a category-based baseline. Their experiments suggest that appearance-based, instance-level context is beneficial. They further propose that this richer context may be an important missing ingredient in scene understanding. The evidence supports the direction of the approach, while the broader claim about its role in scene understanding remains a possibility.
neurips-2009-beyond-categories-the-visua.tldr: Visual Memex models appearance and spatial relationships between individual objects, with experiments suggesting benefits over category-based context.

paragraphs: Sequence labeling assigns labels to positions in an ordered input, and relationships among nearby labels can help determine the right assignments. In practice, models often use only adjacent-label dependencies because incorporating longer sequences makes standard inference expensive. This computational obstacle limits the patterns that a model can conveniently exploit.

The paper shows how a conditional random field can support features that depend on long consecutive sequences of labels while retaining efficient inference. The key condition is that the features involve only a small number of distinct label sequences. Thus, long patterns need not automatically make computation impractical; the variety of patterns represented also matters.

Efficient inference in turn enables efficient learning for these models. Experiments show that high-order features can produce substantial improvements on some problems, and the paper discusses when such features are effective. The contribution provides a conditional route to using richer label dependencies, with benefits tied to the structure of the features and the problem being solved.
neurips-2009-conditional-random-fields-w.tldr: CRFs can efficiently use long label-sequence features when those features contain only a small number of distinct patterns.

paragraphs: The paper develops a rigorous way to build Bayesian models for infinite-dimensional objects, including functions, infinite graphs, and infinite permutations. Such objects go beyond the probability distributions often emphasized in nonparametric Bayesian statistics. The construction starts with finite-dimensional models, providing a route from manageable Bayesian calculations to a model of an infinite object.

Its central contribution extends the Kolmogorov extension theorem to conditional probabilities. This allows systems of finite-dimensional Bayes equations to define nonparametric Bayesian models. The framework also explains how choosing conjugate finite-dimensional models can guarantee a conjugate posterior in the resulting nonparametric model and how to determine its posterior parameter update explicitly.

The authors further show that constructing conjugate models in this way essentially requires exponential-family finite-dimensional components. As an application, they derive a Bayesian model on infinite permutations that extends a model for rank data. The significance is a constructive connection between finite Bayesian specifications and infinite-dimensional inference, including conditions that support useful posterior structure.
neurips-2009-construction-of-nonparametr.tldr: An extension theorem for conditional probabilities constructs infinite-dimensional Bayesian models from finite-dimensional Bayes equations.

paragraphs: The paper studies information carried by patterns of fMRI measurements across multiple voxels. Its method estimates mutual information for a local pattern rather than assessing each voxel separately. This matters because the usefulness of a group of measurements can depend on their joint behavior. The authors report that selecting voxels this way improves decoding accuracy over univariate information selection and other standard selection methods.

They extend the same multivariate perspective to functional connectivity between distributed brain regions. Instead of examining a single measurement from each location, they jointly estimate information shared by two sets of voxels. This provides a way to map relationships between regions under the experimental conditions.

Validation uses an fMRI experiment with six scene categories. The analysis finds strong shared information between PPA and RSC, consistent with existing scene-related neuroscience findings. A whole-brain exploration also identifies other regions sharing information with that network. These additional relationships suggest directions for future neuroscience research.
neurips-2009-exploring-functional-connec.tldr: Joint information analysis of fMRI voxel groups improves decoding and identifies shared information within and beyond a scene-processing network.

paragraphs: The paper learns predictors that choose maximum-weight matchings in bipartite graphs. Its probabilistic model uses an exponential family whose sufficient statistics encode both permutations and observed features. Learning proceeds through maximum a posteriori estimation, connecting the matching problem to a statistical model of possible assignments.

Inference is generally difficult, but the authors identify document ranking as an important application where exact inference is efficient. For general instances, they describe an available sampling approach. This distinction matters because the computational demands depend on the structure of the application, even within the same modeling framework.

The authors establish statistical consistency for their approach and report that its performance improves more favorably with growing sample size than existing max-margin matching models. Applications include computer-vision matching and a standard document-ranking benchmark, where they obtain leading results and improve on max-margin variants. The stated tradeoff is runtime: on large graphs, the method is comparatively expensive relative to max-margin alternatives.
neurips-2009-exponential-family-graph-ma.tldr: A statistically consistent probabilistic matching model achieves strong ranking results, with efficient exact ranking inference but comparatively high runtime on large graphs.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a model for detecting motion contrast: how movement in one spatial region differs from movement in another. It extends phase tuning, a mechanism associated with sensory neurons, to this comparison. The aim is to explain responses to relative movement, which is relevant when a moving region stands out from its surroundings.

The model compares motion-related neuronal responses across two spatial regions through phase shifts. Similar motion corresponds to zero phase shift, while motion differences correspond to nonzero shifts. By constructing differential motion opponency between these responses, the model can detect varying degrees of motion contrast.

Its responses can show either enhancement or suppression depending on surrounding motion, whether that surrounding motion is similar or different. The central advantage is selectivity to relative rather than absolute motion. The authors suggest that this behavior could model neurons observed in neurophysiological studies of motion pop-out. This is a proposed explanatory mechanism for those responses, rather than an established identification of their biological implementation.
neurips-2009-extending-phase-mechanism-t.tldr: A phase-based model compares motion across regions and could explain neuronal responses involved in motion pop-out.

paragraphs: FACTORIE addresses how to express probabilistic models for complex relational data. Such models gain power from repeated structures and shared parameters, but defining those structures flexibly can be difficult. The paper advocates using imperative programming to describe model construction, inference, and learning while retaining the statistical meaning of an undirected factor graph.

This combination lets users express domain knowledge both as relationships in a probabilistic model and as procedures that construct or operate on that model. The authors implement the approach as a library in an object-oriented, strongly typed, functional language. The design links flexible model specification with opportunities for computational efficiency.

In experiments on joint segmentation and coreference, FACTORIE is compared with Markov Logic Networks. The authors report speedups of 3–15 times and error reductions of 20–25%, achieving the leading results reported for that setting. These findings support the practical value of imperative model definitions alongside declarative statistical semantics, particularly for the relational task evaluated.
neurips-2009-factorie-probabilistic-prog.tldr: FACTORIE combines factor-graph semantics with imperative programming, improving speed and accuracy in experiments on joint segmentation and coreference.

paragraphs: The paper investigates Gaussian process regression for functions defined on graph vertices, using large regular random graphs as its main example. It examines random-walk kernels, which specify relationships between function values across the graph. A central question is how those relationships change as the kernel's lengthscale grows.

Under a locally tree-like approximation, increasing the lengthscale does not make neighboring values fully correlated. Instead, the kernel approaches a nonconstant limiting form that the authors calculate. Full correlation appears only when graph loops become relevant. The paper estimates the crossover to that regime, showing why the tree approximation changes the expected large-lengthscale behavior.

The authors also study learning curves relating Bayes error to training-set size. A simple approximation based only on the spectrum of a large tree predicts their qualitative behavior. These curves generally scale with the number of training examples per vertex. The paper then explores how this behavior changes when larger lengthscales make loops important.
neurips-2009-kernels-and-learning-curves.tldr: The paper explains how graph loops affect random-walk kernels and how Gaussian process learning curves generally scale with examples per vertex.

paragraphs: The paper asks which vertices of a graph should be labeled to support prediction at the remaining vertices. It focuses on selecting one batch in advance. The selection process is therefore offline and nonsequential, rather than choosing additional vertices in response to labels already obtained.

The authors derive simple selection methods from graph smoothness assumptions. These assumptions describe how labels vary across the graph, making them directly relevant to whether a chosen set of labeled vertices can support accurate predictions elsewhere. The resulting theoretical bounds express prediction error in terms of the smoothness of the true labels.

Some bounds provide new explanations for previously proposed selection algorithms, while others motivate new algorithms. The authors evaluate those methods and report improvements over baselines on several real-world datasets. The contribution connects a modeling assumption to a practical choice of where to obtain labels: graph structure helps guide selection, and the guarantees explicitly depend on how well the true labels conform to that structure.
neurips-2009-label-selection-on-graphs-1.tldr: Graph smoothness assumptions motivate batch label-selection methods with error bounds and empirical improvements over baselines.

paragraphs: The paper examines both neural signals and the noise mixed into in vivo recordings. One difficulty is that individual neural spikes occupy different frequency ranges, making a single bandpass filter hard to optimize for every spike. The authors propose adapting the filter to the spectrum of each spike instead.

They also investigate multiple noise sources using analytical models and empirical measurements. In their analysis, neuron noise is the dominant contribution, followed by noise at the electrode interface. This suggests that concentrating major noise-reduction effort on the electronics would have limited value in the studied setting.

Measured in vivo noise has a frequency spectrum in the family 1/f^x, with x reported as 1.5 ± 0.5, rather than the conventional white Gaussian description. The authors use noise shaping to reduce this structured noise. Combined with adaptive bandpass filtering, the methods yield several decibels of signal-to-noise improvement. The findings connect noise characterization to concrete choices about filtering and where reduction efforts are likely to matter.
neurips-2009-noise-characterization-mode.tldr: Characterizing spike spectra and recording noise motivates adaptive filtering and noise shaping that together improve signal-to-noise ratio by several decibels.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a directed acyclic graph that describes a data-generating mechanism. Additive noise models are attractive because they need not assume linear relationships or Gaussian data and can sometimes identify a unique graph. However, an earlier multivariate approach enumerated all possible graphs, and invertible cases such as linear Gaussian models cannot be resolved by that approach alone.

The proposed method combines a PC-style search with local additive-noise searches. Kernel measures of conditional dependence guide the first stage. The local searches then examine substructures within the resulting equivalence class, using additive-noise information where it can help distinguish directions.

This combination is more computationally efficient and remains useful for arbitrary distributions, including cases where additive noise models are invertible. That usefulness does not imply unique identification in every case. Experiments on synthetic and real data show greater accuracy than previous methods when relationships are nonlinear and/or data are non-Gaussian. The approach brings complementary sources of structural information into one search procedure.
neurips-2009-nonlinear-directed-acyclic-.tldr: Combining conditional-dependence search with local additive-noise modeling improves efficiency and empirical graph recovery for nonlinear or non-Gaussian data.

paragraphs: The paper presents an online algorithm for learning rotations. A rotation matrix must satisfy specific structural constraints: it is orthogonal and has determinant one. Learning therefore requires more than adjusting matrix entries to improve predictions; the update process must also keep the parameter within the set of valid rotations.

The proposed method uses matrix exponentiated-gradient updates motivated by the Von Neumann divergence. Its additive updates are skew-symmetric matrices with zero trace, belonging to the Lie algebra associated with the rotation group. Matrix logarithms and exponentials connect these updates to the rotation parameter while preserving orthogonality and unit determinant.

The significance of this construction is that the update rule incorporates the geometry of the parameter space. The authors also discuss interpretations involving the computational topology of compact Lie groups, together with stability and computational complexity. The contribution is an online learning procedure designed around rotation constraints, with analysis of how that structure affects its mathematical interpretation and computation.
neurips-2009-on-learning-rotations-3ec40.tldr: An online matrix-update algorithm learns rotations while preserving orthogonality and determinant one through logarithms and exponentials.

paragraphs: The concave-convex procedure solves problems whose objectives are differences of convex functions by repeatedly solving convex subproblems. It is used in methods including sparse and transductive support vector machines and sparse principal component analysis. The paper examines what can rigorously be concluded about the behavior of this iterative process.

The authors argue that the original convergence analysis is incomplete and that deriving the result from the broader difference-of-convex algorithm uses more specialized machinery than CCCP requires. They instead apply Zangwill's general convergence theory for iterative algorithms, obtaining a simpler framework for the proof.

The analysis addresses when CCCP reaches a local minimum or stationary point and when the generated sequence itself converges. These are distinct questions: characterizing possible limiting solutions and establishing convergence of the sequence require separate attention. The paper also identifies an open question about local convergence. Its contribution clarifies convergence reasoning for a widely used procedure without claiming that CCCP universally finds a global optimum.
neurips-2009-on-the-convergence-of-the-c.tldr: The paper uses Zangwill's convergence theory to rigorously analyze when CCCP approaches stationary solutions and when its iterates converge.

paragraphs: Orthogonal matching pursuit is a greedy method for recovering a sparse vector from linear measurements. A k-sparse vector has only k nonzero entries among its n coordinates. The paper sharpens an existing analysis of how many random measurements are sufficient for recovery with probability approaching one as the dimension grows.

The earlier result used 4k log(n) noise-free measurements. The new analysis shows that 2k log(n-k) measurements suffice for asymptotic recovery. This is a stronger sufficient guarantee for the algorithm, reducing the measurement count justified by the theory. It does not establish that this count is necessary for every recovery problem.

The same measurement scaling also suffices to identify the nonzero coordinates in the presence of measurement errors, provided the signal-to-noise ratio tends to infinity. That condition is central to the noisy result. The scaling matches the stated measurement requirement for the more complex lasso, showing that this greedy algorithm can attain the same asymptotic measurement scaling under the analyzed conditions.
neurips-2009-orthogonal-matching-pursuit.tldr: A sharper analysis shows that 2k log(n-k) random measurements suffice for asymptotic OMP recovery, including noisy support recovery when SNR diverges.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning effectively from a single pass through training examples. Second-order stochastic gradient descent can potentially achieve generalization performance comparable to the empirical optimum in that setting. Its practical obstacle is computing the inverse Hessian of the loss, a matrix calculation the authors describe as prohibitively expensive.

Periodic Step-size Adaptation seeks useful second-order information through an approximation. It estimates the Jacobian of a mapping function and uses a linear relationship between that Jacobian and the Hessian. The Hessian approximation is updated periodically, making the timing and construction of curvature information central to the approach.

Experiments across a wide variety of models and tasks report near-optimal results. These findings support the possibility of obtaining much of the benefit associated with second-order learning through periodic approximation. The contribution is a practical adaptation strategy for the single-pass setting; the reported experimental success does not turn the potential of second-order methods into an unconditional guarantee for every learning problem.
neurips-2009-periodic-step-size-adaptati.tldr: Periodic Step-size Adaptation approximates Hessian information through a Jacobian relationship and achieves near-optimal single-pass results in experiments.

paragraphs: The paper explores where to encourage sparsity in an unsupervised latent-variable model. It extends posterior regularization so that the model favors sparse posterior assignments on unlabeled training examples. The distinction is between encouraging sparse inferred explanations of the data and encouraging sparsity in the model's parameters.

The authors apply the method to first-order hidden Markov models for unsupervised part-of-speech tagging. They compare it with ordinary expectation-maximization training and with a sparsity-inducing Dirichlet prior trained using variational EM. This comparison tests whether imposing sparsity through posterior behavior is more useful for the task than the alternative parameter-focused approach.

Evaluation covers English, Bulgarian, and Portuguese under four conditions. Posterior regularization improves on both baselines throughout the reported evaluation, with absolute accuracy gains of 2.5–8.7 percentage points over EM. Improvements also appear when a limited dictionary supplies some supervision. The variational Bayesian alternative degrades performance in most cases, highlighting that the location of the sparsity preference matters in these experiments.
neurips-2009-posterior-vs-parameter-spar.tldr: Encouraging sparse posterior assignments improves HMM part-of-speech tagging across the reported conditions, outperforming EM and a parameter-sparsity approach.

paragraphs: Mapping synaptic connections by stimulating possible input neurons one at a time is slow, especially when most possible connections are absent. RESCUME uses this sparsity to motivate a different measurement strategy: stimulate several randomly chosen candidate input neurons together while recording a receiving neuron's response.

A compressive-sensing decoding algorithm then estimates individual connection weights from the combined responses. The approach promises time savings that increase with circuit size. The authors use computer simulations to choose stimulation parameters and examine feasibility under conditions including measurement noise and nonlinear synaptic integration.

The paper also finds that multiple-neuron stimulation can support reconstruction from postsynaptic spikes when subthreshold voltage measurements are unavailable. It proposes extending the approach by recording many receiving neurons simultaneously with calcium indicators, voltage-sensitive dyes, or multi-electrode arrays. Such parallel measurements could potentially enable reconstruction of an entire circuit. The central contribution is a sparse-recovery measurement strategy supported by simulation-based feasibility exploration, with broader circuit mapping presented as a possibility.
neurips-2009-reconstruction-of-sparse-ci.tldr: RESCUME combines simultaneous random neuron stimulation with sparse recovery to potentially accelerate synaptic circuit mapping.

paragraphs: The paper develops regression methods for outputs that belong to a metric space, where distances are available but ordinary numerical averaging may not be the appropriate operation. It proposes a family of nonparametric kernel-smoothing estimators that includes both a robust median-type estimator and the classical Fréchet mean.

The output space and its distance measure determine which prediction procedure results. Different choices connect the framework to multiclass classification, multivariate Euclidean regression, manifold-valued regression, and some structured-output problems. This gives several seemingly different tasks a shared formulation while allowing their output geometry to affect the estimator.

The authors focus their analysis on regression with manifold-valued inputs and outputs. For manifold-valued outputs, they establish pointwise and Bayes consistency for every estimator in the family. Experiments illustrate robustness properties of the estimator. The contribution combines a flexible construction for geometric outputs with theoretical consistency results in the manifold setting and empirical evidence about resistance to problematic observations.
neurips-2009-robust-nonparametric-regres.tldr: A family of distance-based regression estimators includes robust median prediction and has consistency guarantees for manifold-valued outputs.

paragraphs: The paper uses unlabeled data to construct a compact set of functions for semi-supervised classification. Its foundation is the cluster assumption: high-density regions are sufficiently separated by low-density valleys. Under this condition, each dense region corresponds to a unique representative eigenvector of a kernel matrix.

The method first chooses an appropriate eigenvector basis from unlabeled examples. It then uses labeled examples and Lasso to select a classifier formed from those components. More precisely, the classification functions use Nyström extensions of the eigenvectors. The resulting classifier has a sparse representation, with sparsity arising naturally from the assumed cluster structure.

This separates two roles for the data: unlabeled observations reveal candidate structure, while labels determine how to combine that structure for prediction. Experiments on real-world datasets show performance competitive with leading semi-supervised methods and better than Lasso applied in a kernel PCA basis. The results support the value of choosing a basis that reflects separated clusters when that assumption is appropriate.
neurips-2009-semi-supervised-learning-us.tldr: Under a cluster assumption, unlabeled-data eigenfunctions provide a naturally sparse basis for classifiers selected with labeled data and Lasso.

paragraphs: The paper aims to reduce the setup time for an EEG-based brain-computer interface by removing individualized classifier calibration. It distinguishes this step from placing the electrode cap: dry electrodes can reduce physical preparation, but adapting the system to a user's brain signature introduces another substantial delay.

The authors use motor-imagination EEG recordings from 83 subjects to build a library of subject-specific spatio-temporal filters. From that library, they derive a subject-independent classifier. The approach uses recordings from previous participants to support decoding for a new user, rather than requiring a fresh calibration procedure before that person can begin.

Offline results indicate that users without prior BCI experience could potentially start real-time use without calibration while accepting only a very moderate performance loss. The distinction between offline evidence and the proposed real-time use is important to the finding. The work supports the feasibility of reducing a major setup burden through shared training data, with the usability benefit balanced against the reported decoding-performance reduction.
neurips-2009-subject-independent-eeg-bas.tldr: A classifier built from 83 subjects' EEG recordings shows offline promise for BCI use without individual calibration at a moderate performance cost.

paragraphs: The paper studies sparse linear estimation when the number of variables greatly exceeds the number of noisy observations. Its main result shows that multistage thresholding can accurately estimate the sparse parameter vector under restricted eigenvalue conditions. These conditions support model-selection consistency under weaker requirements than previous results.

The analysis also permits comparatively substantial numbers of nonzero parameters. In particular, the authors identify settings where the method works although ordinary Lasso would fail. This makes the contribution about both accurate estimation and the range of sparse problems for which the theory supports successful variable selection.

A further result concerns the Gauss-Dantzig selector. If the design matrix satisfies a uniform uncertainty principle and the true parameter is sufficiently sparse, its squared-error performance is within a logarithmic factor of an ideal oracle benchmark while selecting a sufficiently sparse model. That oracle knows which coordinates are nonzero and which exceed the noise level. The guarantee therefore measures how closely the method approaches an informed reference under explicit assumptions.
neurips-2009-thresholding-procedures-for.tldr: Multistage thresholding achieves sparse estimation under restricted eigenvalue conditions, with a separate conditional near-oracle guarantee for the Gauss-Dantzig selector.
